headline: Connecticut bottle-deposit law adds criminal penalties for large out-of-state redemptions
dek: A new statute bars people from collecting Connecticut refunds on containers bought elsewhere and allows misdemeanor or felony charges when the volume reaches thousands of bottles or cans.
body: Connecticut's latest bottle-deposit changes took effect Oct. 1, adding criminal penalties to the state's effort to stop people from redeeming large quantities of beverage containers that were purchased somewhere else. [Public Act 26-148](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2026/act/pa/pdf/2026PA-00148-R00SB-00457-PA.pdf) says no person may collect or charge a refund value on a container not purchased in Connecticut, and it applies to conduct the law describes as willful.

The statute sets escalating criminal categories by volume. Willfully redeeming 5,000 to 19,999 out-of-state containers in a calendar year is a Class B misdemeanor under the act. The law identifies 20,000 to 30,999 containers during a one-year period as a Class A misdemeanor, and 40,000 or more as a Class D felony. The published act does not state a separate threshold in the text between 31,000 and 39,999 containers, an omission that could matter if prosecutors try to apply the new scale to a case in that range.

The law is aimed at a problem that grew after Connecticut raised its standard deposit from five cents to 10 cents in January 2024. Connecticut is one of a small group of states with bottle-return programs, while neighboring Rhode Island has no cash-deposit system and New York generally uses a five-cent deposit. That difference can create an incentive to bring containers across a state line and collect Connecticut's higher refund, even though the deposit was never paid here.

[CT Insider](https://www.ctinsider.com/connecticut/article/bottle-deposit-law-changes-october-1-22441604.php) reported Oct. 3 that Connecticut's redemption rate rose sharply after the 10-cent deposit began, then declined as other controls took effect. The [Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/reduce-reuse-recycle/bottles/connecticut-bottle-bill) reported an 85.7% rate for the first quarter of 2026 and 79.6% for the quarter ending June 30, according to the report. Those figures show how many containers were redeemed, but they do not identify how many returns were fraudulent or how many came from outside the state.

The new criminal provision is one part of a broader regulatory response. [DEEP's bottle-bill guidance](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/reduce-reuse-recycle/bottles/connecticut-bottle-bill) says redemption-center owners and operators must obtain a state license beginning July 1, 2026, and submit a $2,500 fee with the application. Earlier changes also created identification and record-keeping requirements for high-volume returns and set daily limits. The rules are designed to give the state more information about who is redeeming containers and how much material passes through each center, although enforcement still requires investigators to connect a person to a large number of containers and show that the conduct was willful.

The law specifically exempts common or contract carriers and warehouse workers who are lawfully transporting or storing beverage containers as merchandise, along with employees acting within that job. That language distinguishes ordinary shipping and distribution from the conduct the statute targets. It also means the new penalties are not a blanket ban on moving beverage containers across state lines; the issue is collecting Connecticut's refund on containers that were not bought in Connecticut.

The dispute has consequences beyond people waiting in redemption-center lines. [CT Insider](https://www.ctinsider.com/connecticut/article/bottle-deposit-law-changes-october-1-22441604.php) described beverage distributors as absorbing handling and refund costs when redemption volumes exceed the number of containers sold in the state. A Bridgeport redemption-center owner told the publication that new scanning equipment could change how quickly his employees process returns and could affect staffing. Connecticut's challenge is to reduce cross-border abuse without making legitimate recycling harder for consumers, charities and businesses that depend on the deposit system.

[DEEP](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/reduce-reuse-recycle/bottles/connecticut-bottle-bill) has said the bottle bill remains an environmental program as well as a financial one: deposits are intended to keep containers out of roads, waterways and landfills and to feed usable material back into manufacturing. The Oct. 1 law therefore starts another phase of a policy experiment that Connecticut began when it doubled the deposit. State officials will have to see whether licensing, identification, scanning and the new criminal thresholds stabilize redemption rates without shifting too much cost onto redemption centers or ordinary residents.
